That the drop is large in some names, small or absent in others, and that a 30% fall erased very different amounts of gain depending on the stock.

sum: AI server stocks are sliding hard ahead of a critical earnings report, and the question hanging over the sector is whether surging revenue can survive a brutal squeeze on margins and cash flow.

AI server stocks are extending the slide that began in the prior session, and Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI | SMCI Price Prediction) is feeling the pressure just before its next earnings report. Super Micro stock is at $31.15, down 5% during the afternoon session. Results are due on November 3.

The group’s slide started on October 30, when Super Micro fell 4% as a broad AI selloff followed a weak outlook from Intel (NASDAQ:INTC). The S&P 500 fell 2% and the NASDAQ Composite dropped 3% that day, while Intel plunged 29% after releasing a weak profit forecast. Over the past month, Super Micro stock is down 23%. Even so, the shares remain up 8% year to date (YTD).

A preview of Super Micro’s Q1 FY2027 results is already out. Super Micro put its preliminary September-quarter revenue at $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, well above Super Micro’s prior guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion. That puts the focus on whether AI infrastructure demand remains durable, whether gross margins hold and whether memory shortages push costs higher.

At its last report on August 11, Super Micro posted a non-GAAP gross margin of 17.6% for Q4 FY2026. Management credited that margin to better customer and product mix, plus contracts deferred into later quarters, lower tariff costs and lower inventory reserves. CEO Charles Liang called the quarter’s revenue shortfall “purely a timing story,” and the company guided Q1 gross margin to 10.4% to 10.8%.

The AI server rival tracking Super Micro most closely is Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL). Dell stock is at $407.98, down 4%. Over the past month, Dell stock has fallen 24%, a steeper drop than Super Micro’s over the same stretch. That decline still leaves Dell up 228% YTD.

Dell reported an AI backlog of $95 billion at the end of its last quarter. On Dell’s September 1 call, Jeff Clarke described the company’s supply limits as “DRAM, DRAM, DRAM, followed by NAND, NAND, NAND.” Memory pressure of that kind could also show up in Super Micro’s margins.

Intel Plunges 25% as Weak Outlook and PC Slump Overshadow Earnings Beat; Dell Tumbles 13%, AMD Sinks 10%, NVIDIA Falls 3%
sum: Intel's earnings beat meant nothing once Wall Street saw what the company expects next, and the fallout is dragging down chipmakers and PC giants alike as a memory crunch reshapes the entire sector's near-term outlook.

A quarterly earnings beat ran into a much weaker outlook. The selloff is erasing a chunk of this year’s rally at Intel (NASDAQ:INTC | INTC Price Prediction). Shares are at $68.85, down 25%, in premarket trading. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX), a fund concentrated in chip stocks, is at $479.97, down 7%. That’s a much steeper slide than the broader Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which is at $697.49, down 2%.

The company reported after the market closed on October 29, and the stock had finished the regular session at $92.07. Wall Street analysts expected adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.41 for Q3 2026, and Intel delivered $0.52. Quarterly revenue at Intel reached $16.5 billion, in line with estimates and up 21% year over year.

Intel disclosed on October 29 that it expects Q4 2026 revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $17 billion Wall Street analysts expected. For adjusted EPS, Intel’s guidance of $0.25 sits well under the $0.43 Wall Street analysts projected. On margins, Intel expects a Q4 gross margin of 38%, down from the 43% it reported in Q3.

A memory-chip shortage is at the center of the problem, pushing up PC prices and squeezing IT budgets. Under that pressure, Intel now projects the PC market will shrink 12% in 2026 and 10% in 2027, with the slowdown lasting at least through the first half of 2027. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said, “We expect the current environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize.”

CFO David Zinsner noted the pressure. “intensified during Q3, particularly late in the quarter, and resulted in a meaningful adjustment in customer purchasing patterns.” An accident in early October also forced an extended shutdown at Intel’s Israel factory, which the company expects to cut roughly $300 million from Q4 revenue.

Lost in the selloff, Intel’s Data Center and AI revenue grew 78% to $7.3 billion, which the company called its strongest growth in 15 years. Sales at Intel Foundry rose 58% to $6.7 billion, while Client Computing Group revenue fell 5% to $8.1 billion.

The firm pointed to rising demand for high-capacity flash storage from large cloud and AI customers. Susquehanna’s case centers on 75TB-plus QLC-based DirectFlash Modules, the dense flash building blocks Pure uses in systems such as FlashArray//E and FlashBlade//S. Large-scale cloud and AI enterprise buyers are looking for more efficient alternatives to hard drives, and that shift favors Pure if those customers keep buying bigger flash modules rather than spinning disk.

Raising the target by $35 signals the firm sees a larger earnings and multiple path if that capacity mix continues to scale.The risk is concentration and timing. Cloud and AI storage budgets can pause even when the long-term flash-for-HDD story remains intact, and a Positive rating still needs successive quarters of DFM demand to validate the higher target.

Everpure’s shares are extremely volatile and have had 35 moves greater than 5% over the last year. In that context, today’s move indicates the market considers this news meaningful but not something that would fundamentally change its perception of the business.

Dell Technologies (DELL) closed Wednesday at $412.68, down 9.80%. The company began the day worth roughly $295.6 billion and ended it worth $266.65 billion, which means about $29 billion went somewhere between the open and the close.

The strange part is that nobody can say what took it. There was no earnings miss, no guidance cut, no filing. Evercore raised the target to $500 from $450 on July 8, then on July 15 reiterated Outperform specifically in response to the CoreWeave report, saying it did not view it as a near-term negative to its thesis. The tape, meanwhile, looked less like news and more like a crowd leaving through one door.

That is the actual question here, and it is more interesting than a headline would be. When a company this size sheds a tenth of its value with no reason attached, either the market found something the fundamentals have not shown yet, or a lot of people owned the same trade.

Some accounts of the session concluded that no confirmed catalyst could be attributed to the move at all. Others pointed to a report that Meta Platforms is developing plans to lease out surplus AI training and inference capacity to enterprise customers, which stoked concern that hyperscale cloud providers may have over-built and could slow future server orders for integrators like Dell. Reports that CoreWeave is exploring hedges against potential memory and storage price declines added pressure across the AI hardware supply chain, since lower memory prices would undercut the scarcity narrative that has supported hardware pricing all year.

The Meta item deserves a specific caveat: it is a report about internal plans, not an announced product, a signed contract, or a company filing. Nothing has been confirmed by Meta. A third-order read-through from another company’s unconfirmed capacity plans to Dell’s order book is a long chain, and every link in it is an assumption.

Then there is the tape. Hewlett Packard Enterprise fell roughly 8% and Super Micro Computer about 5% on the same session, while the Nasdaq-100 ETF slid just 1%, a divergence market commentary read as a positioning event rather than a company-specific headline.

The bull case rests on a backlog that keeps refilling. Dell booked $24.4 billion in AI orders in Q1 alone, sitting on a $43 billion AI backlog with a pipeline at multiples of that figure. Management guided FY27 revenue to $165B to $169B and non-GAAP EPS to $17.90 at midpoint, up 74% YoY.

Operating leverage is showing through. ISG operating margin expanded to 10.5% from 9.7%, while CSG widened to 8% from 5.2%. Our bull-case scenario takes shares to $523.69, a 27.9% return. With 18 Buy ratings against just 1 Sell, Wall Street is largely on board.

- Shares of Dell were hovering around $434 Thursday, marking approximately a 5% decline following the rating cut
Dell Technologies (DELL) saw its shares slip to around $434 on Thursday, falling more than 5% after GF Securities analyst Jeff Pu downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold.
The rating change comes on the heels of an impressive nearly 200% rally in Dell shares following the company’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings release in February.
